items.prompt: In the Eisenhower matrix, what is the recommended action for a task that is both urgent and important?

options.label: Delegate it
Do it right away
Schedule it for later
Delete it entirely

rubric: Urgent and important tasks go in the 'do first' quadrant.
Scheduling is for important but not urgent tasks; delegating is for urgent but unimportant ones.

items.prompt: What is time blocking?

options.label: Writing a daily list of tasks in priority order without times
Turning off messages from other people for part of the day
Reserving set periods in your calendar for specific tasks
Working on one task until it is finished before the next

rubric: Time blocking means assigning tasks to specific calendar periods.
A plain to-do list has no assigned times, which is the main distractor.

items.prompt: Which definition best describes procrastination?

options.label: Taking a planned break between two focused work sessions
Voluntarily delaying a task you intended to do
Choosing the most important task to do first every morning
Declining a request because it falls outside your own role

rubric: Procrastination is voluntarily putting off an intended task.
Prioritising, resting and declining are deliberate planning choices, not procrastination.

items.prompt: In the standard Pomodoro technique, what is one work session followed by?

options.label: 25 minutes of work, then a 5 minute break
90 minutes of work, then a 30 minute break
10 minutes of work, then a 2 minute break
50 minutes of work, then a 10 minute break

rubric: The standard Pomodoro is 25 minutes of work and a short 5 minute break.
Other timings are variants of work/rest cycles, not the standard technique.

items.prompt: In the SMART goal framework, what does the letter T stand for?

options.label: Tested
Team-based
Time-bound
Task-based

rubric: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
The other options are plausible-sounding but not part of the acronym.

items.prompt: Which of the following are commonly used planning tools or methods in time management? Select all that apply.

options.label: An unsorted pile of open requests
The Eisenhower matrix
A to-do list
A sunk-cost ledger
A calendar

rubric: To-do lists, calendars and the Eisenhower matrix are standard planning tools.
A sunk-cost ledger and an unsorted pile are not recognised planning methods.

items.prompt: Leo has an exam in three weeks. Studying for it matters a great deal to him, but nothing forces him to start today. Using the Eisenhower matrix, he labels it important but not urgent. What action does the matrix recommend for this kind of task?

options.label: Delegate it to a classmate
Do it immediately before anything else
Drop it until the deadline gets closer
Schedule a specific time to work on it

rubric: Important but not urgent tasks should be scheduled so they get done before they become urgent.
Doing it immediately is for urgent and important; delaying it risks it turning into a crisis.

items.prompt: Why does checking email only at a few set times of day usually save time?

options.label: Every message gets answered sooner because you reply the moment each one arrives
It cuts the cost of switching attention back and forth
It removes the need to keep any daily task list
It lets you handle several other tasks at once

rubric: Batching reduces context-switching, which wastes focus time.
Batching does not speed up replies and does not replace planning.

items.prompt: A manager gives a team a full week for a task that needs two days, and it fills the whole week. Which idea does this illustrate?

options.label: Early starts always produce better quality results
Tasks take less time the more people are involved
Urgent tasks always get done before due dates
Work expands to fill the time available for it

rubric: This is Parkinson's law: work expands to fill the time allowed.
The other options misstate unrelated or incorrect ideas about effort and deadlines.

items.prompt: Which of these is the best example of a task that is important but not urgent?

options.label: Replying to a casual group chat message from today
Fixing a printer jam a minute before a meeting starts
Exercising regularly to protect your long-term health
Answering a phone call from an unknown number right now

rubric: Long-term health matters but has no immediate deadline, so it is important but not urgent.
The other options are urgent and low in importance, which people often mistake for important.

items.prompt: Why is it sensible to leave buffer time between appointments in a daily schedule?

options.label: Tasks often overrun estimates, and buffers absorb delay
Meetings nearly always finish well before the planned time, so gaps stop you idling
A calendar with visible free gaps shows colleagues you are available for more meetings
Buffers let you fit extra short tasks into the same hour without changing the plan

rubric: People tend to underestimate durations, so buffers stop one overrun from wrecking the day.
Buffers are protection against delay, not a way to cram in work or look busy.

items.prompt: Why is multitasking on two demanding tasks usually less efficient than doing them one at a time?

options.label: Working on two tasks makes each one's deadline later
People only have energy for one task per day
Demanding tasks need more total hours of work than easy ones
Each switch costs refocusing time, so both tasks slow down

rubric: Switching between demanding tasks adds refocusing cost and mistakes.
The distractors state invented limits unrelated to switching costs.

items.prompt: Which of the following are effective ways to handle interruptions while doing focused work? Select all that apply.

options.label: Silence notifications and check them at planned times
Answer every message immediately to stay responsive
Keep all alerts on so nothing important is missed
Set aside focus hours and let colleagues know

rubric: Protecting focus periods and batching notifications reduces interruption cost.
Answering everything instantly or leaving alerts on keeps breaking concentration.

items.prompt: Sana must write a 20-page report due in two weeks. Each evening she opens the document, feels overwhelmed, and does something else instead. Which advice best explains how to reduce her procrastination?

options.label: Break the report into small steps and schedule the first one
Wait until the deadline is close so pressure forces her to start
Work on it for six hours straight each time she begins
Clear every other task from her list before touching the report

rubric: Large tasks feel overwhelming; small scheduled steps lower the barrier to starting.
Waiting for pressure and marathon sessions make avoidance and stress worse.

items.prompt: How should you handle a task that is important but not urgent, such as planning next month's study schedule?

options.label: Leave it off your list until a firm deadline appears
Do it right now, ahead of everything else on your list
Keep it in mind and fit it in whenever you find spare time
Book a protected time slot for it before it becomes a crisis

rubric: Important but not urgent work is scheduled so it gets done before it becomes a crisis.
Distractors confuse importance with urgency, treating non-urgent work as either an emergency or as deletable.

items.prompt: What does the planning fallacy describe?

options.label: Underestimating how long a task takes by picturing the best case
Choosing tasks by how enjoyable they are instead of by their deadlines
Planning so far ahead that the plan is out of date by the time it starts
Overestimating how long tasks take so that every deadline feels safe

rubric: The planning fallacy is the habit of underestimating duration by imagining only smooth progress.
Distractors describe other planning errors (padding, over-planning, preference-based choosing).

items.prompt: Why can time blocking show that a plan is unrealistic when a plain to-do list cannot?

options.label: It caps every list at three tasks so nothing extra can be added
It ranks tasks by how enjoyable they are, so hard ones get dropped
Each task needs a calendar slot, so overload becomes visible
It removes meetings from the day, so all hours become free time

rubric: Assigning tasks to real slots makes the limited hours visible, so overcommitment shows up.
Distractors describe features time blocking does not have, such as task caps or removing meetings.

items.prompt: What is the main benefit of batching similar small tasks, such as checking email at set times instead of constantly?

options.label: It cuts the mental cost of switching between kinds of work
It guarantees that every message is answered the moment it arrives
It lets you skip low-value messages without needing to read them
It makes each single message take less time to deal with

rubric: Batching reduces context-switching costs by grouping similar work.
Distractors claim faster replies, skipping messages, or shorter individual tasks, which batching does not provide.

items.prompt: Why does choosing a tiny first step, like opening the document and typing one heading, help against procrastination?

options.label: It makes starting easy, and momentum often carries you onward
It replaces the need to finish the rest of the task later on
It turns the task into an urgent one with a hard deadline
It shows the task is too big, so it should be removed from the list

rubric: A small first step lowers the barrier to starting, and progress often builds momentum.
Distractors misread the tactic as a way to cancel, skip or artificially deadline the task.

items.prompt: Which of these are urgent but not important tasks? Select all that apply.

options.label: A colleague pings you for a file they could easily find themselves
A sales call rings on your desk phone during your work hours
Booking a long-overdue health check-up for next month
A chat poll about lunch that closes in ten minutes
Drafting next year's personal development plan this week

rubric: Urgent-but-not-important tasks demand quick attention but do little for your own goals.
The development plan and check-up are important but not urgent, so they are common wrong picks.

items.prompt: Priya keeps a to-do list of 25 items and works hard all day, ticking off many small ones. Yet she keeps missing the deadline for her main report. Which explanation best fits this pattern?

options.label: She lacks motivation, so setting tighter deadlines on small items would fix it
She needs a longer list so that nothing is forgotten along the way
She simply has too little time overall, so no system could help her
She treats all items as equal, so deadline-critical work is not done first

rubric: Without ranking by importance and deadline, busy work crowds out the key task.
Distractors blame time, list length or motivation rather than missing prioritisation.

items.prompt: An 8-hour day has 2 hours of fixed meetings. You keep 25% of the remaining time as buffer for surprises. How many hours can you fill with planned tasks?
rubric: 8 - 2 = 6 free hours; 25% of 6 is 1.5 buffer; 6 - 1.5 = 4.5.
Learners picking 6 forget the buffer; 5.5 or 3 come from applying the buffer to the wrong base.

items.prompt: A 12-hour report is due Friday at 5 pm. You want it finished by Wednesday night to leave two buffer days. Working evenly Monday to Wednesday, how many hours per day do you need?
rubric: Three working days from Monday to Wednesday: 12 / 3 = 4 hours per day.
Dividing by four or five days ignores the buffer days; 6 uses two days.

items.prompt: Today you have: (a) a contract fix due at 5 pm today, (b) renewing a gym membership next month, (c) a colleague's chat asking about lunch. What is the best order?

options.label: Fix the contract, reply briefly about lunch, schedule the renewal later
Reply about lunch, then renew the membership, then fix the contract
Renew the membership first so that one item is off the list
Do all three in order of how quickly each can be finished

rubric: The contract is both urgent and important; the lunch reply is quick; the renewal can be scheduled.
Distractors order tasks by speed or ease rather than by deadline and importance.

items.prompt: You are in a 90-minute focus block when a colleague stops by with a non-urgent question. Which response best applies good interruption handling?

options.label: Say you are focused until 11:00 and offer to talk then
Cancel the block, since interruptions are unavoidable at work
Ignore them silently until your block has finished
Answer fully now, then restart the block afterwards

rubric: Deferring politely with a specific time protects focus while respecting the colleague.
Distractors either give up the block, or ignore the person in a way that harms the relationship.

items.prompt: Between two tasks, you open an email that needs a one-minute reply. Applying the two-minute rule, what do you do?

options.label: Flag it and batch it with other emails next week
Delegate it so that you stay on the bigger tasks
Reply immediately instead of adding it to your list
Add it to the list and rank it with the bigger tasks

rubric: The two-minute rule says do tasks that take under two minutes right away, since tracking them costs more.
Distractors add overhead to a trivial task, which the rule is designed to avoid.

items.prompt: You have a high-energy period every morning. Which tasks should you place in it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Working through a hard problem set
Sorting routine messages in your inbox
Filing and labelling receipts
Writing the first draft of a proposal

rubric: Demanding, focus-heavy work belongs in peak-energy time.
Filing and routine sorting are low-effort tasks that suit low-energy periods.

items.prompt: Sam has an exam in 3 days, an essay due in 10 days (about 8 hours of work) and a club meeting tomorrow evening. Sam wants a plan for this week that uses deadlines and importance.

options.label: Revise only on the final night so the material feels fresh
Finish the essay first because it is the biggest task, then start revising
Revise first, go to the meeting, and give the essay short daily slots
Skip the meeting and give all spare time to the essay, revising later

rubric: The exam is the nearest deadline, so it gets priority, while the essay is spread out to avoid a last-minute rush.
Distractors rank by size, drop a cheap commitment needlessly, or delay the most urgent task.

items.prompt: Using the Eisenhower matrix, which task is important but not urgent, and so belongs in a protected time block?

options.label: Planning next quarter's training programme for the team
Drafting the client proposal that is due at 9am tomorrow
Answering a colleague's routine question needed by 3pm
Reorganising old email folders into a new structure

rubric: Important, non-urgent work such as planning is scheduled, not rushed or dropped.
The proposal is urgent and important (do now); the question is urgent but low value; folders are neither.

items.prompt: Your last several reports each took about 50% longer than you first guessed. Your gut estimate for the next similar report is 6 hours. How much time should you schedule?

options.label: 12 hours
9 hours
7 hours
6 hours

rubric: Adjust the estimate using your own history: 6 x 1.5 = 9 hours.
Keeping 6 or adding a token hour ignores the known planning-fallacy pattern.

items.prompt: You think best before noon. You must write a 2-hour analysis, clear 40 minutes of routine email, and attend meetings at 1pm, 2pm and 4pm. Which block plan fits best?

options.label: Email 9:00-9:40, report 3:00-4:00 and 4:30-5:30 around meetings
Report in 30-minute slices between email checks all morning
Meetings first, then the report from 4:30-6:30 after the last call
Report 9:00-11:00, email 11:00-11:40, then meetings as booked

rubric: Place the demanding task in the peak-energy window as one uninterrupted block, with routine work after it.
Other plans fragment the work or push it into low-energy, interruption-prone time.

items.prompt: The task 'Sort out taxes' has sat on your list for weeks without progress. Which rewrite applies the 'next physical action' technique best?

options.label: Finish all tax paperwork before the end of the month
Find last year's return and list which documents are missing
Think about how to get the taxes organised with less stress
Work on taxes for a couple of hours this weekend

rubric: A next action is a concrete, immediately doable step that removes vagueness and starting friction.
The others are vague time slots, goals or intentions rather than a first action.

items.prompt: Colleagues keep dropping by every afternoon with non-urgent questions, breaking your focus. Which application of batching interruptions would work best?

options.label: Answer questions on the spot, but keep each reply under a minute
Set a 3pm open slot and ask people to save questions for it
Shift focus work to quieter evening hours when most colleagues have left
Put on headphones during your busiest afternoons and reply to questions by end of day

rubric: Batching gives interruptions a predictable window, protecting focus while staying available.
Instant replies still fragment attention; ignoring people or shifting to evenings is unsustainable.

items.prompt: You must deliver a report in 10 working days and decide to schedule backward from the deadline. Which steps correctly apply backward scheduling? Select all that apply.

options.label: Order tasks by dependency so each starts when its input is ready
Start with the most enjoyable task and fit the rest into leftover days
Add a buffer for slippage to the total planned duration
Assume each task ends exactly on its estimate, leaving no spare time
Place the deadline first, then reserve time for final review before it

rubric: Backward planning anchors on the deadline, respects dependencies and includes slack.
Enjoyment-first ordering and zero-slack assumptions ignore the structure of the plan.

items.prompt: A project needs 3 hours of research, 4 of drafting, 2 of editing and 1 of final review. You can protect 2.5 focus hours per day, and the deadline is the end of Friday. You will split the work evenly across consecutive working days ending Friday. What is the latest day you can start?

options.label: Thursday
Monday
Wednesday
Tuesday

rubric: Total 10 hours divided by 2.5 hours a day is 4 days, so Tuesday through Friday.
Wednesday or Thursday gives only 7.5 or 5 hours of capacity.

items.prompt: Your day is planned in back-to-back one-hour blocks, yet you finish only about 70% of the planned tasks every day. Which diagnosis best explains this?

options.label: Too few tasks are planned, so adding more blocks per day will fix it
You lack willpower, so each block should be cut to 30 minutes instead
The blocks hold no slack, and estimates ignore overruns and transition time
Time blocking does not suit your job, so a plain list will solve it

rubric: A consistent shortfall points to a planning flaw: no buffers and optimistic estimates.
Adding more work or abandoning blocking leaves the cause untouched.

items.prompt: A week's time log shows 3 hours a day in email and chat, checked every few minutes, and deep work done only in 20-minute fragments. What most likely causes the low output?

options.label: Tasks are too large for one person, so the work should be delegated
Email volume is too high to be cleared in under three hours a day
Frequent checking splits focus, so each return costs restart time
Twenty-minute blocks are too short for most tasks to get started

rubric: Constant checking creates context switches that cost recovery time on every return to deep work.
The log shows a checking pattern, not an unmanageable volume or the wrong task size.

items.prompt: Each morning Dana tidies her inbox, colour-codes her calendar and updates her tracker, then has no time left for the grant draft she dreads. Which analysis is best?

options.label: She is too organised and should drop all planning and just start
The admin work is the real priority, so the grant draft can wait
Her tracker is a poor tool, and a better app would make drafting easier
Low-effort tasks are being used to avoid the aversive, important one

rubric: This is productive procrastination: easy, visible tasks stand in for the dreaded high-value one.
Tool changes or dropping planning do not address the avoidance.

items.prompt: A 12-item to-do list with tasks of very different lengths keeps ending the day with small items ticked and the big ones untouched. Why does the list fail where a calendar would not?

options.label: It hides task duration and reserves no time, so quick items always win
Calendars rank tasks automatically by importance, which lists cannot do
Lists allow too few items, so big tasks are dropped to make space
Lists force a strict order, so the biggest task always comes last

rubric: A plain list shows neither duration nor committed time, so easy ticks beat large tasks.
Calendars do not rank importance; they simply commit time to a task.

items.prompt: Sam always does the task with the nearest deadline first, yet his strategic projects are constantly late and he is always firefighting. Which step in his system is faulty?

options.label: He starts every task on its deadline day, so he needs to batch similar small tasks together
He reviews his list daily, which causes too much reshuffling of tasks
His deadlines sit too close together, so he must negotiate longer ones
He ranks by urgency alone, so important work waits until it turns urgent

rubric: Ranking by urgency alone lets important non-urgent work decay into crises.
Daily review and deadline spacing are not the root of the repeated firefighting.

items.prompt: A manager keeps missing commitments. Her log shows she agrees to requests on the spot, never records them or schedules time, and estimates by gut feeling. Which are root causes rather than symptoms? Select all that apply.

options.label: She estimates by gut feeling without using past durations
She apologises to stakeholders after deadlines pass
She works late on the evening before each deadline
She accepts requests immediately without checking capacity
Commitments are not recorded or given scheduled time

rubric: Unchecked acceptance, unscheduled commitments and uncalibrated estimates generate the misses.
Apologies and last-night work are consequences, not causes.

items.prompt: Priya, a team lead, says yes to every request, and her calendar is packed with meetings. Her own project deliverables slip every week although she works 55 hours. Which analysis best identifies the underlying problem?

options.label: She accepts commitments without testing them against capacity and priorities
She works too few hours, so adding evening time would fix it
Meetings are poorly run, so tighter agendas would fix the slippage
Her project is too big, so splitting it into smaller tasks would fix it

rubric: With no filter, others' requests crowd out her own priority work, so adding hours won't help.
The other options treat surface features rather than the missing commitment check.

items.prompt: A developer blocks 9:00-12:00 daily for focused coding, yet colleagues book meetings into that slot most weeks. Which is the most likely root cause?

options.label: Colleagues do not respect deep work, so the only workable fix is to decline every meeting request outright
Morning is the wrong time of day for focus, so people naturally choose it for scheduling meetings
Three hours is too long a block, so the calendar system automatically treats the time as available
The blocks look like open time on the shared calendar, so colleagues get no signal to avoid them

rubric: Unmarked or visibly free blocks give others no cue; the cause is a visibility and protection gap.
Distractors blame people or timing instead of diagnosing how the block appears to others.

items.prompt: A planner's tasks routinely take about 40% longer than estimated, even after a 20% buffer is added to every estimate. What does this pattern most likely show?

options.label: The flat 20% buffer is too small, so a larger buffer would fix the estimates for tasks of any type
Interruptions are the main cause of the overruns, so the planner should schedule fewer tasks each day
Estimates are accurate but the planner works slowly, so the fix is to work faster and not to re-estimate
Estimates are built from best-case imagined steps, not from records of how long similar tasks took

rubric: Overruns that persist despite buffers point to the estimation method (planning fallacy), fixed by using past actuals.
A flat buffer ignores that error varies by task type; the other options dismiss tracking.

items.prompt: Over a month, a project lead clears 95% of inbox requests on the day they arrive, yet her strategic project is two weeks late. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: She processes email too slowly, so faster handling would free enough time to finish the project
Clearing the inbox daily is itself the fault, so she should check email only once per week instead
The project is poorly scoped, so it would be late whatever her daily routine happened to look like
Others' urgency drives her days, so important but non-urgent project work never gets scheduled time

rubric: She is reacting to urgent requests, crowding out important non-urgent work that has no external prompt.
Other options misattribute the delay to speed, scoping or the daily email habit itself.

items.prompt: 'Prepare annual report' has sat on someone's list for three weeks while they keep finishing smaller tasks instead. Which is the most likely cause of the avoidance?

options.label: The list has too few small tasks, so the momentum needed to begin the large one never builds up
The due date is too far away, so the task feels urgent only once the deadline has been moved closer
Motivation is low, so a reward system is needed before a task of this size can be started
The entry is a vague outcome, not a concrete next action, so starting feels costly and unclear

rubric: An undefined, oversized item has no obvious first step, which drives avoidance; defining the next action removes the barrier.
Distractors treat a task-definition problem as a motivation, list-size or deadline problem.

items.prompt: A support engineer gets urgent tickets about six times a day at unpredictable moments. Why does a rigid hour-by-hour schedule tend to fail for this role?

options.label: Rigid schedules usually fail because of weak discipline, so stricter enforcement of the slots would keep the plan on track
Flexible plans work better because they drop firm deadlines, so interruptions stop threatening most commitments
Unpredictable demand breaks fixed slots after the first interruption; priorities plus buffers absorb the disruption
Hour-by-hour plans are poorly suited to support work, so these engineers should rely on memory rather than planning tools

rubric: Unpredictable interruptions break fixed slots; plans with buffers and priorities absorb them.
Distractors blame discipline, reject planning, or wrongly claim flexibility removes deadlines.

items.prompt: A planner's week is booked to 100% of available hours, and 6 of 10 commitments slip. Which observations point to over-commitment rather than poor discipline? Select all that apply.

options.label: Even the best-protected blocks run over because the planned work exceeds the hours
Slipped tasks are spread across all days and types, not clustered after distractions
Tracked task durations sum to more than the available hours before any interruptions
The planner starts late on most blocks despite having no conflicting items
Most slips follow time spent on social media during planned work blocks

rubric: Diffuse slips, overruns in protected blocks and durations exceeding capacity indicate a plan that cannot fit.
Distraction and late-start patterns would suggest a discipline issue instead.

items.prompt: A manager with an open-door policy ends most days having finished little of her own work, though each interruption lasts only 3-5 minutes. A colleague says short interruptions cost almost nothing. Which analysis best explains her low output?

options.label: Each interruption also costs refocus time afterwards, so many brief ones fragment the day into pieces too short for deep work
Helping the team counts as her own work too, so the day was productive even though it feels unproductive to her afterwards
Open-door policies only reduce output when single interruptions last over 15 minutes, so her case must come from something else
Five-minute interruptions are cheap, so the real cause must be that she works too slowly on her own tasks once she is alone

rubric: Switching costs make brief interruptions far more expensive than their duration, fragmenting focus time.
Distractors ignore recovery time or dismiss the output problem.

items.prompt: Criterion: protect the most value at risk, with only 3 free hours today. Tasks: A) routine vendor email, low value, due today; B) client proposal, high value, due in 2 days, needs 3 hours; C) website typo, 5 minutes; D) review a colleague's draft, due next week. What is the best first move?

options.label: Do A first, because it is the only item due today and the earliest deadline always wins
Clear A and C first, since quick wins free the mind and make the proposal easier to start
Do D first, because colleagues are waiting and helping them builds goodwill for later asks
Start the proposal now, since its high value and short runway mean delay is the costliest

rubric: The proposal combines high value with little slack and a large time need, so it best fits the criterion.
Quick-win and earliest-deadline rules ignore value at risk.

items.prompt: Criteria: a role needs 4 hours of uninterrupted analysis daily, and clients accept replies within 4 hours. Which judgment of the policy 'answer every message within minutes' is best?

options.label: Poor fit: replies need only come once per day, since any more frequent checking destroys concentration
Sound: batching messages delays work for others, so it harms the team more than it helps the individual
Poor fit: scheduled checks every few hours satisfy the 4-hour window while protecting the analysis time
Sound: faster replies always build trust, so analysis work should be fitted around incoming messages

rubric: The stated window makes scheduled batch checks sufficient and protects the required focus time.
Distractors ignore the stated criteria or overcorrect to once-daily checks.

items.prompt: A launch plan has no slack left and a fixed deadline. Judging by likelihood and impact on the deadline, which risk should be addressed first?

options.label: One team member's planned one-day absence on a task that has several days of float
Minor formatting rework that nearly everyone expects and that takes about an hour to fix
A critical-path task that rests on a single optimistic estimate with no fallback if it overruns
A task with two weeks of float that might slip by a few days because of a supplier delay

rubric: Critical-path work with no slack and shaky estimates directly threatens the fixed date.
Other risks are absorbed by float or have low impact.

items.prompt: A team lead must keep staff unblocked (each wait costs a developer about an hour) while protecting her own 3-hour planning block. Which approach best meets both criteria?

options.label: Answer written requests once a week, since batching in that way gives staff everything they need
Hold two short drop-in windows daily and give staff a way to flag true blockers outside them
Keep the door open all day, since unblocking staff always outweighs any planning she could do
Close the door all morning with no exceptions, since a protected block cannot allow any breaks

rubric: Fixed drop-in windows plus a blocker channel serve both criteria.
Other options sacrifice one criterion entirely.

items.prompt: Criterion: reliably meet commitments when about 30% of working time historically goes to interruptions. Which weekly plan is best?

options.label: Schedule 100% of hours in tight blocks, since full planning leaves no gaps for time to be wasted
Schedule 100% of hours with 10-minute gaps between blocks, since short gaps absorb all interruptions
Schedule only 30% of hours, since a lighter plan makes every single commitment certain to be met
Schedule about 70% of hours and keep a ranked overflow list so the remainder absorbs disruptions

rubric: Planning to realistic capacity with a ranked overflow list matches the observed interruption rate.
Full or tiny plans mismatch capacity; short gaps cannot absorb 30% loss.

items.prompt: Which judgments about a 'top three priorities each day' rule are well supported? Select all that apply.

options.label: It forces trade-offs before the day is consumed by reactive requests
It can fail if the three are picked by urgency alone, so periodic review against goals is needed
It suits every role equally, including ones that are almost entirely reactive and unpredictable
It guarantees that the important work gets done, so no weekly planning is required
It removes the need to estimate how long each task will take

rubric: The rule forces early trade-offs, but its value depends on how priorities are chosen and reviewed.
Other options overclaim guarantees or universality.

items.prompt: Two deadlines collide on Thursday: a client report with a contractual late penalty, and an internal slide deck for a meeting that could be moved a day at no cost. You can finish only one by Thursday evening. Using the criteria 'avoid penalties and keep trust', what is the best choice?

options.label: Split time evenly so both are half done, which shows effort on both and avoids favouring one
Finish the deck, because the meeting comes sooner and colleagues will see any delay at once
Finish the report and ask now to move the meeting a day, explaining the reason to attendees
Work late on both without telling anyone, since flagging a problem would reflect badly on you

rubric: The report carries the penalty, and moving the free-to-move meeting early protects both criteria.
Splitting or hiding the problem risks both deadlines and trust.

items.prompt: A team lead's calendar is full of back-to-back meetings, so deep work gets done at night. She must pick one change, judged on two criteria: it protects her best cognitive hours and it keeps her team unblocked. Which is best?

options.label: Block every afternoon as focus time and ask the team to hold all questions until the next morning
Decline all meetings for a month so she can finish deep work, then rebuild her calendar afterwards
Keep the calendar as it is and batch deep work into weekends, since team availability matters most
Protect her peak morning hours for focus and add two short daily office-hour slots for questions

rubric: Protected peak hours plus bounded availability meets both stated criteria.
Declining all meetings or deferring questions a full day blocks the team; weekends ignore the peak-hours criterion.

items.prompt: A manager claims: "Eisenhower matrix quadrant 2 (important, not urgent) work should always beat quadrant 1 work." Judge this claim against the goal of meeting commitments reliably.

options.label: Sound: urgency is only a feeling, so schedules should ignore deadlines and follow importance rankings alone, as deadlines add pressure but no value
Flawed: quadrant 2 should be dropped entirely, since only work with an external deadline reliably gets finished on time in practice
Sound: urgent work is by definition less valuable than strategic work, so it should always be postponed in favour of quadrant 2 tasks
Flawed: a real deadline on important work comes first, and the matrix's value lies in shrinking quadrant 1 over time

rubric: Quadrant 1 items are important and due, so ignoring them breaks commitments; quadrant 2 investment reduces future crises.
Distractors treat urgency as meaningless or importance as worthless.

items.prompt: You must choose how to handle email for a support role where some messages need an answer within 30 minutes, and you also need two hours of uninterrupted analysis daily. Which approach best fits both criteria?

options.label: Check email twice daily at set times and tell customers the response time is now one working day
Close email completely during analysis and reply to everything at the end of the day in one batch
Keep email open all day and answer instantly, doing analysis in the gaps between messages
Mute email during analysis except alerts from urgent senders, and batch the rest hourly

rubric: Alerts for urgent senders plus batching protects focus while meeting the 30-minute limit.
Other options violate either the response window or the focus requirement.

items.prompt: Four planning methods are proposed for a freelancer with unpredictable client requests: (1) a rigid hour-by-hour plan, (2) a weekly plan with about 30% unallocated buffer, (3) a plain to-do list with no dates, (4) planning only the next task. The criterion is meeting client deadlines while absorbing surprises. Which is best?

options.label: The undated to-do list, because flexibility lets you reorder work freely whenever a new client request arrives
The rigid hourly plan, because detailed time slots guarantee every task fits and remove the need to re-plan
The weekly plan with a buffer, because slack absorbs surprises while deadlines stay scheduled
Planning only the next task, because long-range plans become wrong whenever new client requests arrive

rubric: Buffered weekly planning keeps deadlines visible and handles variance.
Rigid plans break under variance; undated lists and next-task planning lose deadline visibility.

items.prompt: A colleague says: "I fixed my procrastination by making my to-do list far more detailed, with 60 items a day." His output has not improved. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: The list is fine; procrastination is a motivation trait, so no change to his planning method can help him much
The list is too short; adding more items would make the unfinished tasks more visible and push him to act on them
The approach is right, but he should reorder items by estimated enjoyment so he starts each day with the easy ones
The long list adds overload and hides the real cause; he should name the task he avoids and shrink its first step

rubric: Detailed lists can become a form of avoidance; addressing the avoided task and first action works.
Distractors add volume, rely on enjoyment ordering or claim it is fixed.

items.prompt: A project manager reviews a plan whose task estimates were all given as single best-case figures and which has no slack before a fixed launch. Which critiques are valid given the goal of reliably meeting the date? Select all that apply.

options.label: Single-point estimates are acceptable if the team is motivated
Best-case estimates ignore variance, so the plan is likely to slip
Adding slack at the end is pointless since tasks expand to fill time
Without slack, one delay on a dependent task moves the launch

rubric: Optimistic point estimates and zero buffer both make slippage likely.
Distractors misuse Parkinson's law or substitute motivation for estimation.

items.prompt: Maya must deliver a report Friday. On Wednesday a manager asks her to join an urgent client call that will take half a day. She has 12 hours of report work left and 14 working hours before Friday ends. Judged on keeping the commitment and the relationship, which response is best?

options.label: Accept the call and skip the report's review step, trusting that the finished draft will be good enough to submit
Decline the call so the report stays on schedule, without explaining the conflict or offering the manager any alternative
Accept the call, then tell the report's owner now the hours no longer fit and negotiate scope or timing
Accept the call and quietly work late to finish everything, avoiding any difficult conversation with the report's owner

rubric: Half a day lost leaves about 8 hours for 12 needed, so early renegotiation is the sound option.
Silent overtime, refusal or skipping review each hide the conflict or cut quality.

items.prompt: Design a weekly planning routine for a new parent working part-time with fixed childcare hours. Constraints: it must fit 15 working hours, protect one deep-work block, and survive unplanned childcare emergencies. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Plan day by day with no weekly view, so each day adapts to whatever childcare demands arise and deep work goes wherever time is free
Plan around childcare hours, put deep work in the first block, and keep 3 hours unassigned as an emergency buffer
Put deep work in the last block of the week and leave no buffer, since urgent items will fill any gaps that open up
Fill all 15 hours with scheduled tasks and handle any emergency by making up the lost time at night when it occurs

rubric: Early deep work, fixed-hour planning and a buffer meet every constraint.
Others lack the buffer, weekly view or protected early deep work.

items.prompt: Create a rule to cut reactive interruptions for a hospital pharmacist. Constraints: urgent clinical calls must always get through, routine queries must stop breaking concentration, and the rule must need no extra staff. Which fits?

options.label: Ask clinicians to send queries by email and have the pharmacist check the inbox at the end of each shift, keeping the phone for emergencies
Log routine queries in writing for two set daily answer windows; clinical calls use a separate direct line
Switch phones to silent during dispensing and have a nearby colleague step in to relay anything that seems urgent
Answer queries as they come, but record each interruption's time and cause so patterns can be reviewed weekly

rubric: It separates urgent from routine channels without extra staff.
Others block urgent contact, ignore the goal or delay clinical communication.

items.prompt: Build a system for a student with five courses, deadlines clustered in weeks 6 and 12, and a habit of starting late. Constraints: work must begin early, hours must be visible, and the system must take under 15 minutes a week to maintain. Which design fits?

options.label: Back-plan milestones from each deadline into one calendar, with a 15-minute Sunday review that books next week's first sessions
Keep a separate notebook and to-do list for each course, and review all five in detail every evening to keep tasks current
Give each course a full-day study block that rotates weekly, deciding what to work on when the day arrives, with no other planning
Set deadline reminders for two days before each due date, so the approaching pressure creates the motivation to begin the work

rubric: Backward planning in one calendar with a short review meets all three constraints.
Others exceed maintenance time or start late.

items.prompt: A team of six repeatedly misses sprint commitments because members take on tasks without checking capacity. Which fix meets: it is based on data, it limits intake, and it needs no new tool?

options.label: Double every estimate going forward, and let people pull in extra tasks from the backlog whenever they finish early
Let each person decide privately how much to take, since individual ownership improves accountability and commitment
Ask everyone to work longer hours in the last days of each sprint so the team closes the gap before the review
Commit each sprint to the average of recent completed work, and require swapping an item out before adding one

rubric: Historical throughput with swap-in rules limits intake using existing data.
Overtime, blanket doubling and private choice do not control capacity.

items.prompt: You have a plan for an executive: calendar blocks for deep work, a daily priority list, and a weekly review. She still misses commitments made verbally in hallway chats. What is the plan missing?

options.label: A longer daily priority list, with an end-of-day recall session to write down any verbal promises she can remember
More deep work blocks each week, so that hallway conversations become less frequent and fewer promises get made
A capture habit that logs each new commitment at once with a due date and routes it into the list
A stricter rule that her team must book meetings in advance instead of raising requests in hallway chats

rubric: Uncaptured commitments never reach the system, so capture is the gap.
Other options avoid the capture problem or damage collaboration.

items.prompt: Design a daily shutdown routine for a remote worker. Constraints: it must stop work creep, reduce next-day startup friction, and catch loose commitments. Which elements should be included? Select all that apply.

options.label: Keep adding tasks to the list until it feels complete, even if that runs past the planned finish time
Write the first concrete action for tomorrow's top task so the next day starts without deciding
Leave email open after hours so that late requests are never missed and nothing slips through
Review open items and move each into the calendar or list, then close the laptop at a set time

rubric: Review catches loose items; a named first action eases startup.
Open email feeds work creep; endless additions do not stop it.

items.prompt: A consultant handles three clients with unpredictable requests, a fixed weekly deliverable for each, and frequent late-day demands. She wants a design that guarantees deliverables, limits late-day disruption, and shows when she is full. Which design fits?

options.label: Keep deliverable work flexible and sort it by whichever client has complained most recently
Block deliverables early in the week, keep a visible request queue, and accept new work only against spare capacity
Handle requests as they arrive and finish each client's deliverable on Friday with whatever time remains that week
Reserve each client a fixed weekday for all their work and decline any request that arrives outside that client's day

rubric: Early blocks, a queue and capacity-based acceptance meet all three goals.
Others risk deliverables, block clients or ignore visible capacity.
